title: Business Cash Advance vs. Loan: Which Fits You?
seo_title: Business Cash Advance vs Loan: Side-by-Side | Fidelity Funding
meta_description: Business cash advance vs loan: compare cost, repayment, speed, qualification and risk side by side, with a simple framework to decide which fits you.
keywords: merchant cash advance vs business loan
dek: Both put cash in your account. They differ in cost, repayment, speed and risk. Here is a decision guide built on the differences that matter.
intro: You need $40,000, and two offers are on the table. One is labeled a loan with a monthly payment. The other is a cash advance with a daily remittance and a number called a factor rate. On the surface they look similar. In practice they behave very differently in your bank account and on your balance sheet.

This guide compares the two across the dimensions that decide real-world outcomes: how they are priced, how repayment works, how fast they fund, who qualifies, and what can go wrong. At the end there is a short framework for choosing.
Terms and availability vary by funding partner and your profile. Nothing here is a guarantee or a quote.

paragraphs: A business loan is a debt: you borrow principal and repay it with interest or fees on a schedule, typically over months or years. A merchant cash advance is generally structured as a purchase of a portion of your future receipts at a discount, repaid through a percentage of sales or fixed debits until a set total is reached.

That legal distinction explains many of the practical ones. Advances commonly use a factor rate rather than interest, often do not have a fixed maturity date and tend to rely less on credit and collateral.
No table is perfect, but these general contrasts hold across many offers, with exceptions by partner.
bullets: Pricing: loans use interest rates or fees; advances use factor rates commonly quoted around 1.1 to 1.5
Repayment: loans often monthly or weekly; advances often daily or as a percentage of card sales
Term: loans from months to years; advances typically a few months to about a year or so
Speed: advances often decide and fund faster; bank loans can take weeks
Qualification: advances weigh deposits more than credit; loans, especially bank ones, weigh credit and history more
Cost: advances usually cost more over a short window in annualized terms

paragraphs: Take a hypothetical $40,000 need. Option one is a 12-month term loan with total repayment of $45,600, paid as $3,800 per month. Option two is an advance at a 1.30 factor, so $52,000 total, paid at about $410 per business day over roughly 127 days. The advance costs $6,400 more in total and takes cash out daily. But if the loan option requires weeks of paperwork and you need the money for a discount that expires Friday, that premium may buy something real.

The right comparison is total dollars paid, the repayment period and the effect on daily cash flow. Do not compare a factor rate to an interest rate directly. A 1.30 factor repaid in four months is far costlier on an annualized basis than a 30 percent annual rate.

Daily debits are steady and relentless: they continue on slow days. Sales-percentage holdbacks flex, so a quiet week costs you less. Monthly loan payments leave your balance intact between due dates but arrive as a large lump, so you need cash set aside for them.

Think about when your money arrives. A business with card-heavy daily deposits, like a restaurant, is naturally aligned with daily remittance. A contractor paid in large milestone invoices may find daily debits awkward and a monthly structure more comfortable.

Both products can include personal guarantees and UCC liens. Advances may include reconciliation provisions that adjust payments if sales fall, though not all do and the mechanics vary. Loans may include collateral requirements, covenants or prepayment penalties. Read the guarantee language, the default triggers and any clauses related to confessions of judgment, whose treatment varies by state.

Stacking is the most common danger with advances: taking multiple at once multiplies daily payments quickly. Loans can also overburden you, but their lower frequency tends to make the burden more visible before it becomes a crisis.
Work through these questions in order. They will usually point you to one answer or at least narrow the field.
steps: How soon do you need the money, in days or in weeks?
Can you qualify for a conventional loan on credit, history and documents?
Will the money pay for itself within the repayment period?
Can your average daily deposits comfortably absorb the payment, including on a slow week?
What is the total dollar cost of each offer, and is the speed premium worth it?

key_takeaways: Loans are priced by interest or fees over a term; advances by a factor rate against future receipts.
Advances usually fund faster and qualify more easily but often cost more in total.
Compare total dollars paid, repayment period and cash-flow fit, never factor rate versus interest rate alone.
Check guarantees, liens, reconciliation and stacking risk in either product.

faq.q: Which is cheaper, a cash advance or a loan?
faq.a: Loans are usually cheaper on an annualized basis, especially bank and longer-term loans. Advances trade higher cost for speed and easier qualification. The honest comparison is total dollars paid over the repayment period, so ask for that figure on every offer. If the speed is not needed, a slower product may save real money.

faq.q: Can I get both at the same time?
faq.a: Sometimes, but combining them increases the total payments leaving your account. Some partners restrict additional borrowing, and others will price it accordingly. Add up every obligation before agreeing to another one. A specialist can add up the combined daily and weekly debits for you.

faq.q: Which is easier to qualify for?
faq.a: Advances generally look harder at deposits and less at credit, so they can be easier for newer or lower-credit businesses. Loans, particularly from banks, weigh credit, history and documents more. Approval is never guaranteed with either. Time in business and revenue consistency matter for both.

faq.q: Does a cash advance build business credit?
faq.a: Often not. Many advance providers do not report to business credit bureaus, while some loans do. If building credit matters, ask whether the funding partner reports payment history before you choose. Reporting practices differ widely, so confirm before relying on a product to build credit.

faq.q: What if my sales drop while I am repaying?
faq.a: With a percentage-of-sales structure, payments typically fall with sales. With fixed debits or loan installments, they do not. Some advances include reconciliation language. Ask how your specific agreement handles a downturn before you sign. Request that language in writing and have it explained if it is unclear.
